slides.title: Research design

fields.line: The Chapter 2 gap becomes one main question, six SRQs and six ROs, staged across CA2 and CA3

slides.notes: In this part I move from the literature review to the research design. Chapter 3 states the research gap, the main research question and the six sub-research questions, SRQ1 to SRQ6. Chapter 4 turns each question into a research objective, RO1 to RO6, and Tables 4.1 and 4.2 map them one to one. RO1 to RO5 each answer one requirement from Section 2.2, Req 1 to Req 5, and RO6 provides the formal and empirical assurance that they are met. The key point is the staging. RO1 to RO4 form the foundational model for the current stage, CA2, and RO5 and RO6 are the principal agenda for CA3. The split reflects research scope and maturity, not a different set of questions.

slides.title: The missing piece is an integrated trust model
slides.subtitle: Research gap (Section 3.1) and main research question (Section 3.2)

fields.statement: How can a trust-oriented computing framework establish and enforce trustworthy multi-party consent for decentralised healthcare data sharing under identity, authority and policy constraints?

support.head: Fragmented mechanisms
support.body: Blockchain consent, DIDs, VCs, policy control and multi-party approval are studied separately, not as one model.

support.head: Consent kept as a record
support.body: Access may rest mainly on a stored record and an authenticated requester, not proven authority, approvals or scope.

support.head: No single source of trust
support.body: Immutability, identity or approval alone cannot make access trustworthy; trust emerges from a verifiable process.

slides.notes: The key point here is that the gap is not a missing technology. Section 3.1 notes that blockchain consent, decentralised identity, verifiable credentials, policy-based authorisation and multi-party approval are each well studied, but usually as independent technical solutions. Against the five requirements, no study meets more than three, and none meets both Req 1, consent as an evaluable object, and Req 3, threshold authorisation. A blockchain can make a consent event immutable without making its participants legitimate, and a valid DID says who someone is, not what they may do. So I treat trust as an emergent property of a verifiable authorisation process. The main research question in Section 3.2 follows from this. Establish covers how participants, authority and collective decisions are created; enforce covers how they are evaluated when a request is made.
slides.issues: To fit 140 characters, the main RQ drops 'computing' and 'for decentralised healthcare data sharing'. The subtitle restores the data-sharing context; the full wording is in Section 3.2.

slides.title: Six questions, six objectives, two stages
slides.subtitle: SRQ1–SRQ6 map one-to-one onto RO1–RO6 (Tables 4.1–4.2); RO1–RO4 in CA2, RO5–RO6 in CA3

rows: Consent as a trust-aware, evaluable authorisation object
DIDs and VCs, with identity separated from authority
RO2: Decentralised Identity and Authority Trust
Verified parties jointly decide; no unilateral authorisation
Policy, purpose and data-scope constraints in authorisation
RO4: Policy- and Context-Aware Access Control
Validity interval, expiry, revocation and state transitions
Formal security properties and empirical validation
RO6: Formal Security Assurance and Empirical Validation

slides.notes: This table condenses Tables 4.1 and 4.2 in Chapter 4. Each sub-research question has one matching objective. SRQ1 and RO1 model consent as an evaluable authorisation object. SRQ2 and RO2 verify identity through DIDs and authority through VCs, as separate conditions. SRQ3 and RO3 require a threshold of independently verified approvals, so no single participant can authorise alone where collective approval is required. SRQ4 and RO4 check purpose and data scope, so a valid identity and enough approvals still cannot reach data outside the consent. These four form the current stage. SRQ5 and RO5 add the validity interval, expiry, revocation and controlled state transitions, and SRQ6 and RO6 add formal analysis and empirical validation through the HALAH prototype, including negative and adversarial testing. Both are next-stage work for CA3.
slides.issues: Two objective names are shortened to fit the 46-character limit. RO2 uses '&' for 'and' (the full name is 'Decentralised Identity and Authority Trust'). RO6 drops 'Security' (the full name is 'Formal Security Assurance and Empirical Validation').

slides.title: Access is a conjunction of trust conditions
slides.subtitle: Eq. 6 decides access now (CA2); Eq. 24 adds temporal and lifecycle checks in CA3

predicates.name: Identity and authority
predicates.meaning: VerifyDID(u) ∧ VerifyVC(u): DID shows who u is, VC shows role or authority (Eq. 8)

predicates.name: Multi-party authorisation
predicates.meaning: Holds only if |A_v| ≥ N verified approvals; |A_v| < N ⇒ DENY (Eqs. 9–10)

predicates.name: Policy and scope compliance
predicates.meaning: R must meet the consent's purpose and scope; S_R ⊈ S_C ⇒ reject (Eqs. 11, 5)

predicates.name: Temporal validity
predicates.meaning: Next stage: t_s ≤ t ≤ t_e, time t lies within the consent's validity interval (Eq. 12)

predicates.name: Lifecycle validity
predicates.meaning: Next stage: ValidState(C) ∧ ValidTransition(C); not expired, revoked or invalid (Eq. 15)

fields.takeaway: Identity is not authorisation (Eq. 1). ALLOW only when every predicate holds; if any one fails, the decision is DENY (Eq. 18).

slides.notes: This slide brings the questions together in one decision rule. The consent object C = (I, A, P, E) from Eq. 7 holds identity information, authority requirements, policy constraints and authorisation evidence. In the current stage, Eq. 6 allows access only when V_I, V_A and V_P all hold. Eq. 24 in Section 3.4 extends this for the next stage with V_T for the validity interval and V_L for the lifecycle state. That matches the extended object C = (I, A, P, T, L, E) already used by the HALAH prototype (Section 7.2). The key point is Eq. 1: identity is not authorisation, so a verified DID does not by itself grant access. Any failed predicate means DENY. SRQ6 is not a sixth predicate; it is the assurance layer that checks these properties formally and empirically.
slides.issues: The V_I name is shortened from 'Identity and authority validity' (31 characters) to fit the 30-character limit.

slides.title: Five requirements for a trustworthy decision
slides.subtitle: Section 2.2: derived from the Chapter 1 problem and the Australian regulatory setting

fields.intro: The framework must meet five requirements for a trustworthy data-access decision; each of the 33 studies is assessed against them.

cards.head: Req 1 Evaluable consent object
cards.body: Structured consent: who may access, under which authority, for which purpose and data, and for how long

cards.head: Req 2 Identity is not authority
cards.body: Verify who the party is, then separately whether they hold the authority the consent requires

cards.head: Req 3 Multi-party threshold
cards.body: Independent approvals from defined participants; consent activates only at a predefined threshold

cards.head: Req 4 Purpose- and scope-bound
cards.body: Requested purpose and data scope evaluated against the consent as a condition of the decision

cards.head: Req 5 Lifecycle validity and audit
cards.body: Expiry, revocation and state checked at each request; evidence of every decision kept for review

slides.notes: Now I set out the five requirements of Section 2.2, drawn from the Chapter 1 problem and the Australian setting: the Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) of the Privacy Act 1988, the My Health Records Act 2012 and the Healthcare Identifiers Act 2010. Req 1 asks for consent that can be evaluated, not just recorded. Req 2 separates identity from authority: a valid credential shows someone is a registered practitioner or legal guardian, not that they are authorised for this patient, this purpose and this data. Req 3 reflects paediatric, aged-care and shared-guardianship settings, where no single party should grant access alone. Req 4 follows the APPs, which limit the use of health information to the primary purpose of collection or a directly related purpose. Req 5 adds expiry, revocation and evidence. Section 2.4 assesses every study against them.

slides.title: 33 studies in six categories
slides.subtitle: Table 2.3: categorisation of the shortlisted studies S1–S33 (Step 4, Section 2.3.6)

points.head: Consent governance leads
points.body: Nine studies stress autonomy and informed consent, but consent remains a record, not an evaluated object

points.head: Security layers stay separate
points.body: Identity (7), access control (7) and blockchain (5) each secure one layer; no single mechanism makes the access decision trustworthy

points.head: Few multi-party studies
points.body: Four multi-party studies and one Trusted Computing study; approval as a consent condition gets less attention

slides.notes: This slide shows how the 33 included studies, S1 to S33 in Table 2.3, fall into six categories. In Step 4 I analysed each paper by its scope, topic area, authors, venue, contribution and limitations, and placed it in one of six areas. Healthcare consent and privacy governance is the largest group with nine studies, then decentralised identity and policy-based access control with seven each, blockchain with five, multi-party governance with four, and a single Trusted Computing study on remote attestation. The key point is that each group builds its own mechanism: as Section 2.4.7 notes, these contributions address different layers of the security problem. I kept five studies from outside healthcare because their mechanisms transfer directly to healthcare authorisation. Integrating trusted execution is left as future work in Section 10.2.

slides.title: No study covers more than three requirements
slides.subtitle: Tables 2.4–2.9: number of studies in each category that address each requirement

fields.takeaway: Req 4 (17 studies) and Req 5 (18) are addressed most often, Req 3 by only three. No study addresses more than three of the five; S7, S22 and S24 reach three.

points.head: Coverage follows category
points.body: Req 1 comes mostly from consent governance (7 of 9) and Req 2 from identity studies (7 of 11)

points.head: Req 3 is the weakest
points.body: Only S15, S23 and S25 address it, and none attaches an approval threshold to the patient's consent

slides.notes: Here I summarise Tables 2.4 to 2.9. Each study is marked as addressing or not addressing each requirement, and the matrix counts those studies per category. Req 4 and Req 5 are the best covered, with 17 and 18 studies, much of that from the blockchain and access-control categories. Req 1 is addressed by nine studies and Req 2 by eleven, but they cluster in the consent-governance and identity categories. Req 3, multi-party threshold authorisation, is addressed by only three studies: S15, S23 and S25. No single study reaches more than three of the five; S7, S22 and S24 reach three, and S1 and S33 reach none. As Section 2.6 concludes, each requirement is addressed in isolation by at least one stream, but no approach combines them into a single, independently verifiable decision.
slides.issues: The per-category counts, the 'no more than three' finding and 'S1 and S33 reach none' are derived from the tick marks in Tables 2.4–2.9 (all verified against the tables); the report text does not state these counts directly.

slides.title: Five gaps, one per requirement
slides.subtitle: Section 2.5: research gaps in the existing studies from the requirement perspective

rows.head: Consent recorded, not evaluated
rows.gap: Nine studies record, encrypt, execute or legally define consent; none carries the conditions to evaluate a later request

rows.head: Identity verified, authority not
rows.gap: Eleven studies establish who a participant is; none verifies the authority a consent requires as a separate condition

rows.head: No threshold on the consent
rows.gap: S15, S23 and S25 offer multi-party mechanisms, but no threshold of verified approvals is attached to the consent

rows.head: Policy not bound to consent scope
rows.gap: Policy follows roles, attributes or risk, not the consented purpose and scope, so approved requesters can exceed it

rows.head: Consent lifecycle not checked
rows.gap: Expiry, revocation and state not evaluated at request time; evidence records transactions, not trust conditions

fields.closing: The gaps map in order to RO1–RO5 (Req 1 to Req 5); RO6 provides formal and empirical validation of the resulting decisions.

slides.notes: Next I turn the coverage into gaps, following Section 2.5. The common thread is fragmentation: a valid blockchain record does not show that legitimate participants made the decision, a verified identity does not imply permission, and sufficient approvals do not keep a request within the authorised purpose or data scope. The gaps map in order onto RO1 to RO5, and RO6 validates the resulting decisions formally and empirically. So the central gap is the lack of an integrated Trust Computing framework that relates these conditions. In the current stage, CA2, the foundational decision is Equation 6: Decision(C, R) = ALLOW if and only if V_I(u) ∧ V_A(C) ∧ V_P(C, R). In the next stage, CA3, I will extend it towards lifecycle trust, formal security assurance, adversarial evaluation and empirical validation with the HALAH prototype.

slides.title: Each stream addresses one layer
slides.subtitle: Table 2.10 (condensed): comparison of the existing research streams and the proposed framework

rows: Patient autonomy, informed consent and controlled data sharing
Consent treated as permission, not an evaluable authorisation object
Tamper-resistant records, distributed auditability and transparency
Immutable records do not establish legitimacy, authority or compliance
Self-controlled identity, verifiable attributes and authentication
Identity and credential validity alone do not authorise access
Collaborative participation and distributed verification or governance
Limited integration between collective approval thresholds, consent and access decisions
Fine-grained restriction by attributes, risk, context and constraints
Policy separated from decentralised identity and multi-party consent
Hardware-supported isolation, execution integrity and attestation
Secure execution does not decide if authorisation conditions suffice
Integrated evaluation: consent, identity, authority, approval, policy
Still to add: lifecycle trust, formal assurance, empirical validation

slides.notes: Table 2.10 puts the six research streams side by side with the proposed framework. Reading across, each stream makes a real contribution: consent governance brings patient autonomy, blockchain brings tamper-resistant records, and identity work brings verifiable attributes. Reading down the limitation column, none of them on its own establishes that a data-access decision is trustworthy. As Section 2.4.7 puts it, a blockchain record does not establish participant authority, a valid DID does not establish access permission, and secure execution does not guarantee that the policy is correct. So my contribution is not to replace these technologies but to relate them within one authorisation process. I kept the framework's own limitation on the slide: lifecycle trust, formal assurance and empirical validation remain for the next stage, CA3.

slides.title: Trusted Authorisation for Multi-Party Patient Consent
slides.subtitle: Healthcare data sharing and the HALAH prototype · CA2 report, Yasir Dhaifallah O Alyoubi
slides.notes: My name is Yasir Dhaifallah O Alyoubi, and this is my Candidature Assessment 2 (CA2) presentation. My research asks how a healthcare data-access decision can be trusted when several independent parties, such as a patient, a guardian and a healthcare professional, take part in consent. I will cover the background and literature review, the research design, the architecture and proposed solution, the HALAH prototype and its evidence, and finally my progress and the plan for the next stage. One idea runs through the whole talk: a valid identity is not valid authority.

slides.title: Background and literature

fields.line: Consent is recorded, not evaluated; none of the 33 studies combines all five requirements in one decision

slides.notes: This first part sets up the argument. In Chapter 1 I describe the research context, including the Australian regulatory setting, and the problem. Consent is usually stored as a record, but the record does not necessarily show that the participants were legitimate, that they held the required authority, that all of them took part in the decision, or that a later request stays within the conditions originally authorised. Chapter 2 is the systematic literature review. It defines five key requirements and shortlists 33 studies published between 2022 and 2026, through a four-step process that follows PRISMA 2020. The review shows that at least one stream of research addresses each requirement on its own, but no existing approach combines them into one independently verifiable authorisation decision.

slides.title: The core problem
slides.subtitle: Section 1.2: consent often remains a passive artefact, separate from the access decision

fields.statement: Identity is not authority; recorded consent is not evaluated consent

support.head: Identity without authority
support.body: An immutable record does not prove participants were legitimate; authentication does not prove authority

support.head: One party acting alone
support.body: Guardians, clinicians or institutions may also need to approve; one participant should not decide alone

support.head: Requests beyond scope
support.body: A verified, approved professional may still request data outside the purpose or scope the patient authorised

slides.notes: This slide states the core problem from Section 1.2. Existing approaches usually represent authorisation through database records, access-control entries, smart contracts or blockchain transactions. That improves integrity, traceability and auditability, but consent itself often remains a passive artefact. The key point here is the gap between representing consent and enforcing authorisation in a way that can be trusted. First, immutability protects the record but does not show the participants were legitimate, and authentication identifies an entity but does not give it authority over a particular patient's information. Second, when guardians, healthcare professionals or institutional authorities also take part, no single participant should decide alone. Third, even with verified identities and enough approvals, a request can still exceed the authorised purpose or data scope. What is missing is one integrated mechanism that connects these conditions.

slides.title: Who shares healthcare data, and under which rules
slides.subtitle: Sections 1.1, 2.2, 2.4.1 and 5.1: authorisation as a distributed governance problem in the Australian setting

fields.intro: Several independent parties take part in healthcare data sharing, and no single participant may hold enough authority to decide access alone.

cards.head: Patients
cards.body: Initiate consent and should have greater control over how their data is accessed, shared and reused

cards.head: Guardians, authorised parties
cards.body: Hold part of the authority in paediatric, aged-care and shared-guardianship settings

cards.head: Healthcare professionals
cards.body: A valid credential shows a registered practitioner, not authority for this patient, purpose and data

cards.head: Institutions and auditors
cards.body: Institutions may hold part of the authority; auditors inspect authorisation evidence and audit history

cards.head: Privacy Act 1988 and APPs
cards.body: Sensitive information: collect with consent (APP 3); use for primary or directly related purpose (APP 6)

cards.head: My Health Records and HI Acts
cards.body: My Health Records Act 2012: consumers control provider access; Healthcare Identifiers Act 2010: IHI, HPI-I, HPI-O

slides.notes: This slide summarises the research context from Section 1.1, with the participant roles drawn from Sections 2.2, 2.4.1 and 5.1. Healthcare data sharing involves patients, guardians, healthcare professionals and institutional authorities, and no single participant may have enough authority to decide access alone. That is why I treat authorisation as a distributed governance problem, not just authenticating a user and checking a static permission. The last two cards show the Australian setting. Under the Privacy Act 1988, health information is sensitive information; APP 3 ties collection to consent, and APP 6 ties use to the primary or a directly related purpose. The My Health Records Act 2012 lets consumers control which provider organisations can access their record, and the Healthcare Identifiers Act 2010 governs the national identifiers. HALAH reflects this through purpose-bound consent, module-level data scope and a jurisdiction attribute that defaults to AU.
slides.issues: Section 1.1 does not describe each stakeholder's role in detail, so the four stakeholder cards also draw on Sections 1.2, 2.2.2, 2.2.3, 2.4.1 and 5.1.1. Section 1.1 does not name auditors as stakeholders; that card rests on 2.2.3 (institutions hold part of the authority) and 5.1.1 (the auditor interface supports inspection of authorisation evidence and audit history).

slides.title: Research scope and progression
slides.subtitle: Table 1.1: four objectives in the current stage, two in the next stage

items.name: Temporal and Lifecycle Trust
items.desc: Validity periods, expiration, revocation and controlled consent-state transitions

items.name: Formal Security Assurance and Empirical Validation
items.desc: Formal security and authorisation properties; empirical evaluation with negative and adversarial scenarios

fields.takeaway: CA2 lays the foundations of trustworthy multi-party authorisation; CA3 extends it over time and validates it formally and empirically

slides.notes: Table 1.1 shows how the research is split into two stages. In the current stage, CA2, I work on four foundational dimensions: RO1, a trust-centric consent model; RO2, decentralised identity, with authority kept separate from identity; RO3, multi-party authorisation among independently verified participants; and RO4, policy- and context-aware access control, which stops valid identities and approvals from reaching data beyond the authorised scope. The next stage, CA3, adds RO5, temporal and lifecycle trust, because a consent that was valid when approved can later expire or be revoked. It also adds RO6, formal security assurance and empirical validation of the complete HALAH implementation, including negative and adversarial scenarios.

slides.title: Architecture and solution

fields.line: MVC separates security state, interaction and enforcement; a workflow and an algorithm for each of RO1–RO6

slides.notes: In this part I move from the research design to the solution. Chapter 5 presents the research architecture, a layered Model-View-Controller design. The Model holds the trust and governance state, the View lets independent stakeholders submit or inspect operations, and the Controller evaluates the trust predicates and produces the decision. Chapter 6 then presents the solution objective by objective, with a workflow, a step-by-step procedure and an algorithm for each of RO1 to RO6. RO1 to RO4 belong to the current stage, CA2, and RO5 and RO6 belong mainly to the next stage, CA3. The key point I want to carry through this part is that MVC itself is not the security claim. Security comes from placing trust-sensitive operations in the Controller, structuring security state in the Model and keeping security decisions out of the View.

slides.title: Every sensitive decision passes through the Controller
slides.subtitle: Section 5.1: the View submits claims, the Controller decides, the Model holds security state

points.head: View: interaction boundary
points.body: Role interfaces for patients, guardians, healthcare professionals and auditors; actions are claims, not decisions

points.head: Controller: enforcement
points.body: Validates requests; verifies DID, VC and authority; checks threshold and policy; decides; generates audit evidence

points.head: Model: security state
points.body: DIDs, credentials, consent objects, approvals, policy and scope, evidence, lifecycle; state is not permission

slides.notes: Here I show Figure 5.1, the layered MVC architecture of HALAH from Section 5.1. The View has role-specific interfaces for patients, guardians or other authorised participants, healthcare professionals and auditors. Anything submitted there I treat as a request or claim, not a trusted outcome. The Controller is the security enforcement boundary. It coordinates request validation, decentralised identity verification, credential and authority verification, multi-party approval evaluation, policy and data-scope evaluation and final authorisation, and it generates audit evidence. The Model holds the security state, but a consent, credential or approval record does not by itself produce an access decision. Protected healthcare data sit outside the three layers and are reached only through the Controller. As Section 5.1.4 says, I do not claim that MVC itself provides security. Section 7.10 maps each layer to the code.

slides.title: Access requires every trust predicate to hold
slides.subtitle: Figure 5.3, Table 5.1: the Controller checks V_I, V_A, V_P, V_T, V_L; any false predicate gives DENY (Eq. 18)

points.head: Authority separation
points.body: Identity and authority evidence checked separately; authentication alone does not authorise

points.head: Multi-party authorisation integrity
points.body: Threshold on verified approvals; no unilateral access when collective approval is required

points.head: Policy-bounded access
points.body: Purpose and requested scope checked against the consent; approvals cannot exceed its scope

points.head: Authorisation evidence
points.body: Verification results, approvals, policy outcome and decision recorded for both ALLOW and DENY

slides.notes: This is Figure 5.3, from Section 5.1.2, which shows how the Controller evaluates the trust predicates using evidence held in the Model. V_I checks identity and authority, V_A the approval threshold, V_P purpose and data scope, V_T time validity and V_L lifecycle state. The integrated decision is Eq. 24, and if any required predicate is false the decision is DENY, as in Eq. 18. Both successful and unsuccessful decisions are associated with authorisation evidence. The four points are four of the six security properties in Table 5.1, Section 5.9. The other two are identity-dependent participation and the separation of interaction and enforcement. The key point I want to make is that these properties come from the interaction of the three layers, not from any single technology. V_T and V_L are the next-stage extension; the current-stage decision is Eq. 6.
slides.issues: Four of the six Table 5.1 properties chosen (authority separation, multi-party authorisation integrity, policy-bounded access, authorisation evidence); the other two are named in the notes. 'Multi-party integrity' shortens the property name 'Multi-party authorisation integrity' to fit the 28-character limit.

slides.title: From consent specification to audited decision
slides.subtitle: Section 5.2: consent becomes an evaluable authorisation object, checked before data are released

points.head: Consent specification
points.body: Patient defines purpose, permitted data scope and conditions: the policy context for later requests

points.head: Identity and authority
points.body: DIDs and VCs establish identity and claimed role or authority; this alone does not grant access

points.head: Multi-party approval
points.body: Independent approvals collected; unless |A_v| ≥ N (Eq. 9), the process ends in DENY

points.head: Policy, decision and audit
points.body: Purpose and S_R ⊆ S_C checked; V_I ∧ V_A ∧ V_P (Eq. 6) decides; ALLOW and DENY both recorded

slides.notes: Here I walk through Figure 5.4, the end-to-end workflow in Section 5.2. It puts into practice my premise that trustworthy access cannot come from a single mechanism, such as a blockchain record or an authenticated identity. First, the patient specifies purpose, scope and conditions. DID and VC verification establishes identity and authority, but this alone does not grant access to patient data. Next, the required participants, for example a patient with one or more guardians, give independent approvals, and if the threshold is not met the request is denied. Policy evaluation then catches a legitimate participant asking for data outside the consent, such as the request in Eq. 4, which adds Observation to a consent for Medication and Procedure. The decision is the conjunction in Eq. 6, and both granted and denied decisions are recorded in the audit layer.

slides.title: RO1: consent as an evaluable object
slides.subtitle: Section 6.1 and Algorithm 1: the consent sets the conditions a later request is evaluated against

points.head: C = (I, A, P, E)
points.body: I = identity, A = authorisation requirements, P = purpose and data-scope policy, E = authorisation evidence

points.head: Validate, then construct
points.body: Patient, doctor, guardians, purpose, scope S_C and interval T checked; t_e must be later than t_s

points.head: Algorithm 1: C or REJECT
points.body: Does not grant access directly; assigns id_C, persists C and records creation evidence for audit

points.head: Prototype status
points.body: Patient, doctor and guardian checks (Steps 1–3) not yet enforced at creation; VC authority checks in CA3; t_e > t_s check (Step 6) implemented

slides.notes: With RO1 I answer SRQ1 by turning consent into a structured and evaluable authorisation object, C = (I, A, P, E), from Eq. 7. Figure 6.1 shows the creation workflow. In HALAH the patient selects a patient DID, an authorised doctor, guardian DIDs, data modules such as Observation, Medication, Condition and Procedure, and a start and expiry time. Algorithm 1 validates these inputs and returns the consent object C or REJECT. It does not grant access directly; it sets the conditions that RO2, RO3 and RO4 later evaluate through I, A and P. On status, Section 6.1.2 is explicit. Steps 1 to 3 are not yet enforced at creation, a syntactic DID check is applied later at guardian approval and doctor access, and credential-based authority validation is scheduled for Stage 2, CA3. Step 6, the time check, is implemented.

slides.title: RO2: identity is not authorisation
slides.subtitle: Section 6.2 and Algorithm 2: DID and VC checks yield V_I(u), an input to RO3 and RO4, not an access grant

points.head: DID and VC verification
points.body: DID resolved and verified, then VC signature, issuer, subject and validity period checked

points.head: Authority match
points.body: Extracted role and authority claims must satisfy the consent's requirement A_C, otherwise INVALID

points.head: Output: V_I(u)
points.body: Algorithm 2 returns VALID or INVALID and records evidence; it does not grant access by itself

points.head: Prototype status
points.body: Guardian DID syntax check; EIP-712 approval signatures; W3C VC verification scheduled for CA3

slides.notes: With RO2 I answer SRQ2, and it rests on Eq. 1: identity is not authorisation. A DID gives an identity reference and a VC gives evidence of role or authority, and neither grants access on its own. Figure 6.2 and Algorithm 2 resolve and verify the DID, retrieve and verify the VC, and check the extracted claims against the consent's authority requirements, returning INVALID at the first failure. In HALAH this happens in two steps. The guardian DID is checked for syntax, and the approval is an EIP-712 typed-data signature over the consent identifier that counts only if the recovered address matches the address bound to that DID. For the demonstration, guardian keys are derived from the DID. Full W3C VC verification is specified but scheduled for Stage 2, CA3, so I do not yet verify credential-based authority.

slides.title: RO3: no unilateral activation below the threshold
slides.subtitle: Section 6.3, Figure 6.3, Algorithm 3: only verified, eligible, non-duplicate approvals enter A_v

points.head: Threshold condition
points.body: V_A(C) = 1 when |A_v| ≥ N (Eq. 9), with 1 ≤ N ≤ |G|; below N the consent stays PENDING

points.head: Rejected approvals
points.body: Invalid identity or authority, participant not in G, or a duplicate approval: recorded, returns DENY

points.head: Activation evidence
points.body: When |A_v| ≥ N: authorisation activated, token evidence generated, threshold-satisfied event recorded

points.head: Prototype: 2-of-2 guardians
points.body: N = |G| (all guardians sign); EIP-712 signatures verified, duplicates refused, Sepolia SBT minted; configurable k-of-n in CA3

slides.notes: In this part I present RO3, which answers SRQ3. The key point is that the threshold counts only approvals that pass three checks. Algorithm 3 first verifies the identity and authority of the approving participant, then checks that the participant belongs to the required set G, and then refuses a second approval from the same participant. Each failure is recorded and returns DENY. Only an approval that passes all three is added to A_v. If |A_v| ≥ N, the authorisation is activated and a threshold-satisfied event is recorded; otherwise the consent stays pending. In HALAH, N equals |G|, so with two guardians one signature leaves the consent in PENDING_SIGNATURE, and two signatures plus the SBT mint activate it. The SBT represents the consent state; it is not the source of trust. This is Section 6.3 and Figure 6.3.

slides.title: RO4: a valid approval is not unlimited access
slides.subtitle: Section 6.4, Figure 6.4, Algorithm 4: purpose and data scope are checked before any data are released

points.head: Ordered checks
points.body: V_I(u), active consent, |A_v| ≥ N, purpose, then scope; any failure is recorded and returns DENY

points.head: Scope containment
points.body: S_R ⊆ S_C (Eq. 25), with V_P = V_U ∧ V_S (Eq. 32); returned data must also stay within S_C

points.head: Prototype: scope enforced
points.body: Only consented modules offered; service layer re-checks S_R ⊆ S_C; a failure is logged as ACCESS DENIED

points.head: Prototype: purpose partly checked
points.body: Consent purpose checked against {Treatment, Research, Emergency}; P_R ⊨ P_C comparison is CA3 work

slides.notes: Here I move to RO4, which answers SRQ4. The point is that a legitimate doctor with a valid, fully approved consent may still ask for too much. Algorithm 4 checks identity, consent state and the threshold first, and only then purpose and scope, before any data are released. For example, the request in Eq. 4 adds Observation to a consent for Medication and Procedure, so it must be denied. In HALAH the scope check is enforced in the doctor interface and again in the service layer, and a failure is written to the audit log. Purpose is only partly implemented: the requester does not yet declare a purpose, so the comparison is planned for CA3. Routing the release gate through the full decision matrix is a small planned change. This is Section 6.4 and Figure 6.4.

slides.title: RO5: an existing consent is not always usable
slides.subtitle: Primarily CA3. Section 6.5, Figure 6.5, Algorithm 5: V_T(C, t) and V_L(C) extend the decision (Eq. 24)

points.head: Two added predicates
points.body: V_T(C, t): t_s ≤ t ≤ t_e (Eq. 12); V_L(C): valid state and valid transition (Eq. 15)

points.head: Prototype: state order
points.body: REVOKED, PENDING_SIGNATURE, PENDING_TOKEN, NOT_STARTED, EXPIRED, ACTIVE; only ACTIVE releases data

points.head: Prototype: revocation
points.body: Patient revocation sets REVOKED and calls revoke() on the contract; v3 enforces the interval on-chain

points.head: Remaining for CA3
points.body: Specification of legal state transitions, formal analysis of Eqs. 20–21, and adversarial evaluation

slides.notes: RO5 answers SRQ5 and belongs primarily to the next stage, CA3; Figure 6.5 shows the planned workflow. The key point is that an existing consent is not necessarily usable: once it has expired or been revoked, it must not stay usable just because its approval threshold was once met. Algorithm 5 checks the time interval, whether the current state permits the operation, whether the consent has been revoked, and whether the requested transition is permitted; any failure returns INVALID. HALAH already has a first version: the consent engine checks states in a fixed order, only ACTIVE releases data, V_T is computed in the decision matrix, and a patient revocation calls revoke() on the consent contract. One notation point: the prototype labels a jurisdiction check VL; it will be renamed V_J, so V_L means lifecycle validity. This is Section 6.5.

slides.title: RO6: successful execution is not proof of security
slides.subtitle: Primarily CA3. Section 6.6, Figure 6.6, Algorithm 6: observed decisions tested against formal properties

points.head: Three scenario classes
points.body: S = S_valid ∪ S_negative ∪ S_adv: legitimate workflows, rule violations and bypass attempts

points.head: Six properties
points.body: P_sound, P_deny, P_threshold, P_policy, P_scope, P_audit; every ALLOW needs V_I ∧ V_A ∧ V_P (Eq. 33)

points.head: Observed vs expected
points.body: A scenario passes only when D_obs(s) = D_exp(s); each failure is traced to its condition and evidence

points.head: Implementation basis
points.body: HALAH logs consent, approval, minting, state-check and access events (Sections 7.11–7.12)

slides.notes: RO6 answers SRQ6 and is the assurance layer. It belongs mainly to the next stage, CA3, and is only partly done so far. The key point is that a system can return data without showing that it should have. So Algorithm 6 defines six expected properties, then runs three scenario classes: valid workflows; negative cases such as expired or revoked consent and out-of-scope requests; and adversarial cases such as replayed or duplicate approvals and forged credentials. A scenario passes only when the observed decision equals the expected one, and the evidence is kept so a failure can be traced back to its condition. Formal reasoning defines what the framework should guarantee, and testing checks whether the implementation does. The current HALAH evidence in Sections 7.11 and 7.12 is my starting point. This is Section 6.6 and Figure 6.6.

slides.title: Six algorithms, one authorisation lifecycle
slides.subtitle: Section 6.7: Algorithms 1–4 form the current stage (CA2); Algorithms 5–6 extend them in the next stage (CA3)

rows: I_p, doctor D, guardians G, P_u, S_C, T
2: DID and VC Identity and Authority Verification
RO2: Decentralised Identity and Authority Trust
Consent C, approval a, threshold N
RO4: Policy- and Context-Aware Access Control
Consent C, request R, participant u
Consent C, time t, transition q
RO6: Formal Security Assurance and Empirical Validation

slides.notes: This table brings the six algorithms together, as Section 6.7 does. Each algorithm maps to one objective, and together they form a progressive structure. Algorithm 1 builds the consent object but grants no access. Algorithm 2 turns DID and VC evidence into V_I, Algorithm 3 turns verified approvals into V_A, and Algorithm 4 checks the specific request against purpose and scope before data are released. Together these give the current-stage decision in Eq. 6. Algorithms 5 and 6 are next-stage work for CA3: temporal and lifecycle validity complete Eq. 24, and formal and empirical validation tests whether the whole lifecycle keeps its security properties. The point I want to leave you with is that blockchain contributes integrity and auditability, but trust comes from all of these conditions holding together.

slides.title: HALAH prototype and evidence

fields.line: Four role-based subsystems, the code mapping, 18 automated tests and consent tokens anchored on Sepolia

slides.notes: This brings me to Part D, which is Chapter 7 of the report. So far I have described the model and the six algorithms. In this part I show how the current-stage (CA2) mechanisms are realised in the HALAH prototype. I start with an overview of the four subsystems, then walk through the patient, guardian, doctor and auditor views using the screenshots in Figures 7.1 to 7.5. After that I show how the MVC layers map to the source code in Table 7.2, the automated test results in Table 7.3, and the consent tokens anchored on the Sepolia testnet in Table 7.4. I close the part with the limitations in Section 7.13, because they define what the next stage, CA3, still has to demonstrate.

slides.subtitle: A role-based consent management platform that operationalises the framework (Sections 7.1, 7.8–7.10)

points.head: Patient: create consent

slides.notes: This slide gives the overview of HALAH, from Sections 7.1 and 7.8 to 7.10. The platform is role-based: patient, guardian, doctor and auditor all work on the same consent lifecycle, and the blockchain and cryptographic mechanisms sit inside the workflow rather than being shown as separate components. Figure 7.6 traces one consent through the four views. The consent is stored as PENDING_SIGNATURE, guardians sign EIP-712 approvals until N = |G| is reached, and then the SBT is minted and the consent becomes ACTIVE. The doctor gets access only when the state is ACTIVE, the access proof is valid and S_R ⊆ S_C. The figure also shows which events each step writes to the audit log, and Table 7.1 maps the framework components to the subsystems that implement them.

items.label: Guardian: Cryptographic Approval
items.body: Each guardian verifies their DID and signs; at 2/2 approvals the SBT is minted and the consent is fully activated

slides.notes: Here I show the first two subsystems. On the left is the patient's Create Smart Consent Contract module, from Section 7.2. The patient sets the Patient DID, the Authorised Doctor DID, the data access scope as EMR modules such as medication and procedure, the designated guardian DIDs, and the start and expiry time. Together these build the consent object C = (I, A, P, T, L, E), so consent is bound to a specific subject and a specific actor, and the guardians are part of it from the start. On the right, from Section 7.3, each guardian enters the Consent ID, selects their Guardian DID and signs. The consent is not activated just because the patient created it. Only when both signatures are present is the SBT minted and the consent fully activated.

slides.notes: This slide is the doctor side, from Section 7.4. In Figure 7.3 the doctor enters an authorised Consent ID and the system shows the patient DID, the consent ID, the purpose and the current state, here ACTIVE, with the authorised data scope of Medication and Procedure. Holding a Consent ID is not enough, because the system first checks that the authorisation is still valid. In Figure 7.4 the doctor selects the modules to request, the system verifies the request and reports Access Granted, and only the MEDICATION and PROCEDURE records are released. The key point is that consent and data access are separate events: consent, then verification, then the access decision. In version 1 the integrity proof is a placeholder until the zero-knowledge circuit is built.

slides.notes: The fourth subsystem is the auditor view, from Sections 7.5 to 7.7. It first gives aggregate indicators: 21 total events, 3 consent events and 3 access requests, with Blockchain Integrity shown as VERIFIED. The Consent Lifecycle section in Figure 7.5 then reconstructs the chain of evidence: the patient creates the consent, guardians A and B sign, the smart contract mints the SBT, the Consent Engine checks the state, and the doctor's DATA_ACCESS is GRANTED. Repeated state checks are left out of the figure, and on this slide I have arranged its six event blocks in time order, numbered 1 to 6. The Detailed Audit Records give the event-level evidence, and the Complete Blockchain Audit Ledger records the whole lifecycle, not only successful access. The key point is that this gives the evidence base for accountability, traceability, integrity and non-repudiation.

slides.notes: In Table 7.2, from Section 7.10, I map the MVC architecture of Chapter 5 onto the code at repository commit 0a960ca of 22 September 2026, so the architectural claims can be checked against the source. slides.notes: Table 7.3 in Section 7.11 gives the automated test evidence. The suite was run with pytest 9.1.1 on Python 3.11 on 28 September 2026: 16 tests passed, 2 were skipped and none failed. T1 checks that a valid EIP-712 approval is accepted and that a wrong guardian, a wrong consent ID or a missing signature is rejected. T2 checks that the decision matrix returns ALLOW when all conditions hold and that each tested violation fails the corresponding predicate. T3 and T4 cover the lifecycle and revocation. The two Groth16 tests are skipped because the circuit is not built. These are functional tests with a mocked blockchain, giving initial evidence for SRQ1 to SRQ4 and the first SRQ5 checks. Stage 2 (CA3) still has to add insufficient approvals at the release gate, a duplicate approval, an out-of-scope request submitted directly to the service interface, and a request with a mismatched declared purpose.

fields.line: Where each objective stands, the publication plan and the next-stage (CA3) work on RO5 and RO6

slides.notes: This brings me to Part E, which covers Chapters 8 to 10. Having shown the architecture and the HALAH evidence, I now report where each research objective stands, what I plan to publish and what the next stage will add. The key point here is the split between the two stages. RO1 to RO4 form the current stage, CA2, and have been implemented at prototype level. RO5 and RO6 belong to the next stage, CA3, although a first version of RO5, covering expiry and revocation, already runs in the prototype. I will go through Chapter 8 objective by objective, then Table 9.1 on publications and Table 10.1 on the research plan.

slides.notes: Chapter 9 sets out three research outputs, summarised here from Table 9.1. The first is the Trust-Centric Consent Framework paper on the model architecture and multi-party authorisation policies. The draft is complete and I plan to submit it to Computers and Security, published by Elsevier, in November 2026. It is the core architectural contribution and addresses SRQ1 to SRQ4. The second covers the HALAH prototype, the empirical validation platform, with its decentralised implementation and functional security evaluation; it is aimed at a systems or security conference and is in progress. The third, formal security and lifecycle analysis of temporal constraints and state transitions, is planned for a specialised workshop or journal as the next-stage extension. So the current stage lays the foundation, and the next stage adds formal analysis and empirical validation.

slides.title: Next-stage plan: four research focuses
slides.subtitle: Section 10.2, Table 10.1: whether trust can be maintained over time, formally justified and demonstrated

steps.head: Temporal and lifecycle trust
steps.body: Add validity periods, expiry, revocation and controlled transitions; confirm consent is still valid at access
steps.outcome: A mechanism that checks whether consent is still active at the point of access

steps.head: Formal security assurance
steps.body: Define security properties; analyse invalid identity, too few approvals, policy violation, expiry, revocation
steps.outcome: A formal security model with explicit security guarantees

steps.head: Empirical validation
steps.body: Extend HALAH with positive and negative scenarios; measure runtime, overhead and enforcement accuracy
steps.outcome: Empirical evidence and benchmark datasets on enforcement

steps.head: Integrated evaluation
steps.body: Combine temporal, lifecycle, formal and empirical modules; evaluate interactions, scalability and feasibility
steps.outcome: One integrated, validated framework for multi-party consent

slides.notes: Here I follow Section 10.2 and Table 10.1: the four focuses of the next stage, CA3, in order. First, temporal and lifecycle trust, because a consent that was valid when approved may no longer be valid when it is used. Second, formal security assurance: explicit security properties, analysed under invalid identities, insufficient approvals, policy violations, expired or revoked consent and illegal transitions. Third, empirical validation in HALAH, checking that ALLOW is produced only when all trust conditions hold and DENY otherwise, and measuring runtime, overhead and enforcement accuracy. Fourth, which appears only in Table 10.1, is integrated end-to-end evaluation. Under Eq. (35), the final decision is ALLOW only when identity and authority, multi-party approval, policy, and temporal and lifecycle validity all hold; a denial should keep enough evidence to explain its reason.

fields.intro: No single mechanism makes access trustworthy. The contribution is one explainable decision built from independently verifiable conditions.

cards.head: Evidence and path to CA3
cards.body: Initial evidence: 16 tests passed, SRQ1–SRQ4; CA3 adds lifecycle trust, formal assurance, empirical validation

slides.notes: To conclude, I bring the contributions together, drawing on Chapters 1, 5 and 10 and the conclusion in Section 2.6. The review found that each requirement is addressed in isolation, but no existing approach combines them into one independently verifiable decision. My response has four parts. The conceptual model treats consent as an evaluable object and makes access the conjunction of V_I, V_A and V_P. The MVC architecture routes every sensitive decision through the Controller, so neither the interface nor a stored record can decide access on its own. HALAH implements these conditions at prototype level in a decentralised healthcare setting. The evidence so far is functional; CA3 adds temporal and lifecycle trust, formal assurance and empirical validation, moving from static consent management to dynamic trustworthy authorisation.
